Throughout, "measurable" means $\Sigma$-measurable, and for a measurable $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ and $A\in\Sigma$ we write $\int_A f\,d\mu=\int f\mathbf 1_A\,d\mu$. We use only standard facts about integrals of nonnegative functions: additivity ($\int(f+h)=\int f+\int h$), $\int c f = c\int f$ for $c \ge 0$, monotonicity, and the Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT). In particular, for measurable $f\ge 0$ the map $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\mu$ is a measure (countable additivity follows from MCT applied to $f\mathbf 1_{\bigcup_{k\le n}A_k}$). Absolute continuity $\nu\ll\mu$ means: $A\in\Sigma$, $\mu(A)=0\Rightarrow\nu(A)=0$.

## Step 1. A lemma on finite signed measures

**Lemma.** Let $\lambda,\rho$ be finite measures on $(X,\Sigma)$, put $\sigma=\lambda-\rho$ (a real-valued countably additive set function), and let $E\in\Sigma$ with $\sigma(E)>0$. Then there is $P\in\Sigma$, $P\subseteq E$, with $\sigma(P)>0$ and $\sigma(B)\ge0$ for every measurable $B\subseteq P$.

*Proof.* Call $F\in\Sigma$ *positive* if $\sigma(B)\ge 0$ for all measurable $B\subseteq F$. Put $E_0=E$. Recursively, for $k\ge1$: if $E_{k-1}$ is positive, stop. Otherwise some measurable $B\subseteq E_{k-1}$ has $\sigma(B)<0$, hence $\sigma(B)<-1/n$ for some positive integer $n$; let $n_k$ be the least positive integer such that there is a measurable $B\subseteq E_{k-1}$ with $\sigma(B)<-1/n_k$, choose such a set $B_k$, and put $E_k=E_{k-1}\setminus B_k$.

The sets $B_k$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $E$, and $\sigma(E_k)=\sigma(E)-\sum_{i\le k}\sigma(B_i)\ge\sigma(E)>0$.

If the process stops at stage $k$, then $P=E_{k-1}$ works.

Otherwise we obtain infinitely many $B_k$. Let $B=\bigcup_k B_k$ and $P=E\setminus B$. Since $\lambda,\rho$ are finite measures, $\sigma(B)=\sum_k\lambda(B_k)-\sum_k\rho(B_k)=\sum_k\sigma(B_k)$, a convergent series of real numbers. Its terms are negative, so $\sum_k 1/n_k\le\sum_k|\sigma(B_k)|=|\sigma(B)|<\infty$; hence $n_k\to\infty$. Also $\sigma(P)=\sigma(E)-\sigma(B)\ge\sigma(E)>0$. Suppose some measurable $C\subseteq P$ had $\sigma(C)<0$. Choose $k$ with $n_k\ge2$ and $1/(n_k-1)<|\sigma(C)|$. Since $P\subseteq E_{k-1}$, $C$ is a measurable subset of $E_{k-1}$ with $\sigma(C)<-1/(n_k-1)$, where $n_k-1$ is a positive integer; this contradicts the minimality of $n_k$. So $P$ is positive. $\blacksquare$

## Step 2. Existence when $\mu$ and $\nu$ are finite

Assume $\mu(X)<\infty$, $\nu(X)<\infty$, $\nu\ll\mu$. Let
$$\mathcal F=\Big\{f:X\to[0,\infty]\ \text{measurable}:\ \int_A f\,d\mu\le\nu(A)\ \ \forall A\in\Sigma\Big\}.$$
$0\in\mathcal F$, so $\mathcal F\neq\varnothing$.

*$\mathcal F$ is closed under $\max$.* Let $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal F$, $h=\max(f_1,f_2)$ (measurable). For $A\in\Sigma$ put $A_1=A\cap\{f_1\ge f_2\}$, $A_2=A\cap\{f_1<f_2\}$, disjoint measurable sets with union $A$. Then $\int_A h\,d\mu=\int_{A_1}f_1\,d\mu+\int_{A_2}f_2\,d\mu\le\nu(A_1)+\nu(A_2)=\nu(A)$.

*A maximal element.* Let $\alpha=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_X f\,d\mu\le\nu(X)<\infty$. Pick $f_n\in\mathcal F$ with $\int_X f_n\,d\mu\to\alpha$, and let $g_n=\max(f_1,\dots,f_n)\in\mathcal F$. Then $g_n\uparrow g$ pointwise for some measurable $g:X\to[0,\infty]$. By MCT, for each $A\in\Sigma$, $\int_A g\,d\mu=\lim_n\int_A g_n\,d\mu\le\nu(A)$, so $g\in\mathcal F$; and $\alpha\ge\int_X g\,d\mu=\lim\int_X g_n\,d\mu\ge\lim\int_X f_n\,d\mu=\alpha$. So $\int_X g\,d\mu=\alpha$.

*The remainder vanishes.* Define $\lambda(A)=\nu(A)-\int_A g\,d\mu$ for $A\in\Sigma$. Since $g\in\mathcal F$, $0\le\lambda(A)\le\nu(A)<\infty$; being the difference of two finite measures (countable additivity follows by subtracting two convergent series), $\lambda$ is a finite measure, and $\lambda\ll\mu$ because $\lambda\le\nu$ and $\nu\ll\mu$.

Suppose $\lambda(X)>0$. Let $\varepsilon=\lambda(X)/\big(2(\mu(X)+1)\big)>0$; then $\varepsilon\mu(X)<\lambda(X)/2$, so $\sigma=\lambda-\varepsilon\mu$ satisfies $\sigma(X)>0$. By the Lemma (with $\rho=\varepsilon\mu$, $E=X$) there is $P\in\Sigma$ with $\sigma(P)>0$ and $\lambda(B)\ge\varepsilon\mu(B)$ for every measurable $B\subseteq P$. We have $\mu(P)>0$: otherwise $\lambda(P)=0$ by $\lambda\ll\mu$, whence $\sigma(P)=0$. Let $g'=g+\varepsilon\mathbf 1_P$ (measurable, $\ge0$). For $A\in\Sigma$,
$$\int_A g'\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu+\varepsilon\mu(A\cap P)\le\int_A g\,d\mu+\lambda(A\cap P)\le\int_A g\,d\mu+\lambda(A)=\nu(A).$$
So $g'\in\mathcal F$, but $\int_X g'\,d\mu=\alpha+\varepsilon\mu(P)>\alpha$ (as $\alpha<\infty$), contradicting the definition of $\alpha$. Hence $\lambda(X)=0$, so $\lambda\equiv0$, i.e. $\nu(A)=\int_A g\,d\mu$ for all $A\in\Sigma$.

*Finite values.* $N=\{g=\infty\}\in\Sigma$ and $\int_X g\,d\mu=\nu(X)<\infty$; since $\int_X g\,d\mu\ge c\,\mu(N)$ for every $c>0$, $\mu(N)=0$. Replace $g$ by $\tilde g=g\mathbf 1_{X\setminus N}:X\to[0,\infty)$, measurable. For each $A$, $g\mathbf 1_A$ and $\tilde g\mathbf 1_A$ differ only on the $\mu$-null set $N$, so $\int_A\tilde g\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu=\nu(A)$. (Indeed $\int_A g = \int_{A\setminus N} g + \int_{A\cap N} g$ and $\int_{A\cap N} g\,d\mu=0$ because $A \cap N$ is null.) This proves existence in the finite case.

## Step 3. Existence in the $\sigma$-finite case

*A common partition.* By $\sigma$-finiteness there are $A_k,B_j\in\Sigma$ ($k,j\in\mathbb N$) with $\bigcup_k A_k=X=\bigcup_j B_j$, $\mu(A_k)<\infty$, $\nu(B_j)<\infty$. The countable family $\{A_k\cap B_j\}_{(k,j)\in\mathbb N^2}$ covers $X$, and each member has finite $\mu$- and $\nu$-measure. Enumerate it as $C_1,C_2,\dots$ and set $X_n=C_n\setminus\bigcup_{m<n}C_m$. Then the $X_n$ are pairwise disjoint measurable sets with $\bigcup_n X_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<\infty$, $\nu(X_n)<\infty$.

*Localized measures.* Define $\mu_n(A)=\mu(A\cap X_n)$ and $\nu_n(A)=\nu(A\cap X_n)$. These are finite measures on $(X,\Sigma)$ and $\nu_n\ll\mu_n$ (if $\mu(A\cap X_n)=0$ then $\nu(A\cap X_n)=0$). Moreover, for every measurable $f\ge0$,
$$\int f\,d\mu_n=\int f\mathbf 1_{X_n}\,d\mu. \tag{$*$}$$
Indeed, for $f=\mathbf 1_E$ both sides equal $\mu(E\cap X_n)$; by linearity $(*)$ holds for nonnegative simple $f$; for general $f$ take simple $0\le s_k\uparrow f$, so $s_k\mathbf 1_{X_n}\uparrow f\mathbf 1_{X_n}$, and apply MCT to both sides.

By Step 2 there is a measurable $h_n:X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\nu_n(A)=\int_A h_n\,d\mu_n$ for all $A$, i.e. by $(*)$, $\nu(A\cap X_n)=\int h_n\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}\,d\mu$.

*Gluing.* Define $g=\sum_n h_n\mathbf 1_{X_n}$. Since the $X_n$ partition $X$, at each $x$ only the term with index $n$ such that $x\in X_n$ can be nonzero, so $g(x)=h_n(x)\in[0,\infty)$ for the unique $n$ with $x\in X_n$; $g$ is measurable as the pointwise limit of the measurable partial sums. For $A\in\Sigma$, by countable additivity of $\nu$ and MCT (applied to the increasing partial sums of the nonnegative series $\sum_n g\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}=g\mathbf 1_A$),
$$\nu(A)=\sum_n\nu(A\cap X_n)=\sum_n\int h_n\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}\,d\mu=\sum_n\int g\mathbf 1_{A\cap X_n}\,d\mu=\int g\mathbf 1_A\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu,$$
using $h_n\mathbf 1_{X_n}=g\mathbf 1_{X_n}$. This proves existence.

## Step 4. Uniqueness

Let $g_1,g_2:X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $\int_A g_1\,d\mu=\int_A g_2\,d\mu=\nu(A)$ for all $A\in\Sigma$. Take the sets $X_n$ from Step 3 (only $\nu(X_n)<\infty$ and $\bigcup X_n=X$ are needed). Fix $n$ and let $A=X_n\cap\{g_1>g_2\}\in\Sigma$. On $A$, $g_1=g_2+(g_1-g_2)$ with both summands nonnegative and finite, so by additivity
$$\int_A g_1\,d\mu=\int_A g_2\,d\mu+\int_A(g_1-g_2)\,d\mu .$$
Both $\int_A g_1\,d\mu$ and $\int_A g_2\,d\mu$ equal $\nu(A)\le\nu(X_n)<\infty$, so $\int_A(g_1-g_2)\,d\mu=0$. For each $k\ge 1$ let $A_k=A\cap\{g_1-g_2>1/k\}$; then $\frac1k\mu(A_k)\le\int_A(g_1-g_2)\,d\mu=0$, so $\mu(A_k)=0$. Since $g_1-g_2>0$ on $A$, $A=\bigcup_k A_k$, hence $\mu(A)=0$. Therefore $\mu(\{g_1>g_2\})\le\sum_n\mu(X_n\cap\{g_1>g_2\})=0$. By symmetry $\mu(\{g_2>g_1\})=0$. Thus $\mu(\{g_1\neq g_2\})=0$, i.e. $g_1=g_2$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. $\blacksquare$
